title: Monitor and manage food safety in perishable produce exportation

lessons.title: Intrinsic parameters, the cold chain and food safety hazards
lessons.html:
Intrinsic parameters of perishable produce

Intrinsic parameters are the properties of the produce itself that affect whether micro-organisms can grow on it. Key parameters are:

  • Water activity: fresh fruit and vegetables have high water content, which supports microbial growth.
  • pH (acidity): acidic fruit such as citrus and many berries resists most bacteria but supports moulds and yeasts. Less acidic produce such as melons, leafy greens and sprouts can support pathogens like Salmonella and Listeria.
  • Nutrient content: sugars in ripe fruit feed micro-organisms.
  • Natural barriers: intact skin or rind protects the flesh. Wounds, cracks and cut surfaces remove this protection.

Dangers of breaking the cold chain

Low temperatures slow the growth of most spoilage organisms and many pathogens, and slow the physiological ageing that weakens natural barriers. A break in the cold chain causes:

  • faster growth of decay organisms and, on some products, pathogens;
  • condensation on cold fruit moved into warm air, creating wet surfaces where microbes multiply;
  • faster softening and splitting, opening wounds;
  • failure of cold treatments that depend on continuous low temperatures.

Note that Listeria can grow at refrigeration temperatures, so cold alone does not make produce safe; hygiene remains essential.

Hazards and their impact

TypeExamplesImpact
BiologicalE. coli, Salmonella, Listeria, hepatitis A, norovirus, mycotoxin-producing mouldsFoodborne illness, outbreaks, recalls
ChemicalPesticide residues above MRLs, unapproved actives, post-harvest chemical misuse, cleaning chemicals, lubricants, heavy metalsRejections, market alerts, consumer health risk
PhysicalGlass, metal, hard plastic, wood, stones, jewelleryInjury, complaints, recalls
AllergensCross-contact in facilities that also handle nuts or other allergensSevere reactions in sensitive consumers

A food safety manager must assess which hazards are reasonably likely for each product and process, and focus controls on them.

lessons.title: Managing GAP and GMP for food safety
lessons.html:
How GAP enhances food safety

Good agricultural practices prevent contamination at source, which is far more effective than trying to remove it later.

  • Water: risk-assess every water source; test irrigation and especially post-harvest water at the frequency your certification requires; treat water that contacts produce.
  • Soil amendments: use properly composted manure, applied in a way and at a time that prevents contact with the edible part.
  • Animals: exclude livestock and limit wildlife access to production areas near harvest.
  • Agricultural remedies: use products registered under Act 36 of 1947, follow labels, respect pre-harvest intervals and check market MRLs; keep full spray records and run residue monitoring.
  • Worker hygiene: toilets and hand-washing facilities, training, and a policy for ill workers.
  • Harvest containers and equipment: cleaning programmes and dedicated use.

Monitoring and managing GMP in handling and storage

GMP in the packhouse and cold store covers facilities, equipment, people and processes. The manager's role is to set standards, monitor compliance and act on deviations.

  • Facilities: building condition, pest proofing, protected lighting, drainage, separate areas for chemicals and waste.
  • Process water: dump tanks and drenches monitored for sanitiser concentration and changed on schedule, because recirculated water can spread pathogens and decay.
  • Equipment: food contact surfaces cleanable and cleaned; maintenance that does not contaminate product.
  • Personnel: hand washing, protective clothing, no jewellery, no eating on the line, illness reporting.
  • Storage: product off the floor, correct temperature, stock rotation and separation from chemicals.
  • Transport: clean, pre-cooled vehicles and containers.

Monitoring tools

  • Daily pre-start inspections by supervisors.
  • Records of sanitiser concentration, water tests and temperatures.
  • Trend reviews to spot repeated problems.
  • Corrective action reports with root cause and follow-up.

Managers should walk the floor regularly. Records that always look perfect but do not match what you see on the floor are a warning sign.

lessons.title: Hygiene management systems and food safety audits
lessons.html:
Establishing a hygiene management system

  1. Prerequisite programmes: cleaning and sanitation, pest control, personal hygiene, water management, glass and hard plastic control, waste management, maintenance and training.
  2. Hazard analysis: apply HACCP principles to identify significant hazards and any critical control points, with critical limits, monitoring, corrective actions, verification and records.
  3. Written procedures: sanitation standard operating procedures for each area and machine, including chemical, concentration, method, frequency and responsible person.
  4. Verification: visual checks, swab tests or ATP tests of food contact surfaces, water and product testing where appropriate.
  5. Training and competence: induction and refresher training, with records.
  6. Document control: current versions of procedures available where needed.

Managing the system

Assign a food safety team, set targets, review results monthly during the season, and update procedures when products, processes, equipment or market requirements change. Plan for incidents with a recall and traceability procedure, and test it with a mock recall at least once a year.

Conducting a food safety audit

  1. Plan: define scope, standard or checklist, auditors, date and areas.
  2. Opening meeting: explain the purpose and schedule to the packhouse manager.
  3. Gather evidence: observe operations, interview workers, check records such as cleaning logs, water results, pest control reports, training and temperature records, and trace a lot from carton back to orchard.
  4. Evaluate: compare evidence with requirements and grade findings as critical, major or minor.
  5. Closing meeting: present findings honestly and clearly.
  6. Report: write up findings, evidence and required corrective actions with deadlines.
  7. Follow-up: verify that corrective actions are effective.

Example: during an audit, the auditor finds the dump tank sanitiser log complete, but a test on the spot shows concentration well below the procedure's level. This is a significant finding: the monitoring is not reliable. The corrective action must address both the dosing and the checking method.

Key points

  • Intrinsic properties such as moisture, pH and skin integrity affect microbial risk.
  • Breaking the cold chain speeds decay and can cause condensation and treatment failure.
  • GAP prevents contamination at source; GMP controls handling and storage.
  • A hygiene system needs prerequisites, HACCP, procedures, verification and training.
  • Food safety audits gather evidence, grade findings and verify corrective action.

options.text: No pathogen can grow when cold

quiz.question: Why is recirculated dump tank water a food safety concern?

options.text: It can spread pathogens and decay if sanitiser is not maintained

quiz.question: What happens when cold fruit is moved into warm, humid air?

options.text: Condensation forms, creating wet surfaces where microbes multiply

quiz.question: During an audit, a log looks complete but a spot test shows low sanitiser concentration. What does this suggest?

options.text: The test kit is always wrong
